newsitem.title: NORWAY: Int'l oil group secures exports for Caspian oil.
newsitem.headline: Int'l oil group secures exports for Caspian oil.

text.p: The international consortium developing three giant oilfields offshore Azerbaijan has secured export routes for early production, boding well for the future of its $12-billion project and others in the oil-rich Caspian region, the consortium's president said on Friday.
First oil will flow in September next year, Terry Adams, president of 12-company Azerbaijan International Operating Co (AIOC), told Reuters in an interview.
"It's amazing what has been achieved...it looks like we'll deliver this as a fast track project," said Adams, who was in Stavanger for the 1996 Offshore Northern Seas conference.
AIOC has agreements with Russia and Georgia to transport early production, starting at 100,000 barrels per day (bpd), via two separate pipelines to the Black Sea, Adams said.
The first pipeline to the Russian port of Novorossiisk will be up and running by the end of the year.
The 100,000 bpd line will initially carry oil for Azerbaijan state oil company SOCAR until AIOC oil starts pumping next year.
AIOC has invested $70 million in refurbishing the moribund pipeline and reversing the direction of flow, Adams said.
Carving a corridor through Georgia will take up to two years at a cost of $275 million. This requires connecting a hodge podge of existing elderly pipes with some 800 illegal taps, Adams said.
The Georgian route to the Black Sea port of Batumi is the consortium's preferred export route for the 700-800,000 bpd of "big oil" from the offshore fields.
"In terms of distance, cost and political balance, I think it's our best option," said Adams.
This would require the construction of a brand new pipeline with a huge two million bpd capacity, to serve the export needs of the whole South Caspian region.
The project will be presented to the Georgian government for approval mid-1997.
Adams admitted that securing a route to the Black Sea was not the end of the consortium's export concerns.

He said that given additional volumes of oil from Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan via the proposed CPC pipeline, the overcrowding of Turkey's Bosphorus Straits would become a legitimate environmental concern.
"We would like to see a bypass (pipeline) built...we'll choose the one that gives us the biggest bang for our buck," he said.
Turkey's proposed bypass route from Georgia to Ceyhan on the Mediterranean is being challenged by a route through Bulgaria and Greece.
"If Turkey wishes to see the Bosphorus solution in a pipeline to Ceyhan then it needs to provide the commercial incentive." Adams said.
The development of the 3.8 billion barrel Azeri, Chriag and Guneshli fields is now in the appraisal stage and the first well should be spudded in early September.
The "so far so good" success of the project has attracted new companies to the politically-unstable region, said Adams.
"The Japanese...traditionally very conservative...joined (the consortium) in July 1996, paying an entry fee three times higher than was first paid in 1994."
Two new contracts, for the Karabakh and Shakdeniz fields, followed the AIOC signing and Adams expects more to follow.
Royal Dutch/Shell Group, Chevron Corp, Mobil Corp and Total SA "are all actively in discussion," he said, "and several smaller companies are looking at the onshore."

AIOC comprises SOCAR (10 percent), Amoco Corp (17 percent), Pennzoil Co (4.8 percent), Unocal Corp (10 percent), Exxon Corp (8 percent), British Petroleum (17.1 percent), Ramco Energy Plc (2.1 percent), Russia's LUKoil (10 percent), Statoil (8.6 percent), the Turkish Petroleum Corp (6.8 percent), Itochu Corp (3.9 percent) and Saudi Arabia's Delta Nimir (1.7 percent).
